title: Spring Security Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision notes on the Spring Security filter chain, authentication vs authorization, SecurityFilterChain config, password encoding, stateless JWT auth, method security, CORS and CSRF.

chapters.title: Filter Chain and Auth Model
points: Security is a chain of servlet filters: DelegatingFilterProxy hands each request to FilterChainProxy, which picks the first matching SecurityFilterChain
Authentication = who you are (401 Unauthorized when missing or invalid); authorization = what you may do (403 Forbidden when authenticated but denied)
Key filters in order: SecurityContextHolderFilter, CorsFilter, CsrfFilter, authentication filter (e.g. UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter or a custom JWT filter), AuthorizationFilter last

Authentication flow: filter builds an Authentication token, AuthenticationManager (ProviderManager) asks AuthenticationProviders, which use UserDetailsService and PasswordEncoder, and the result is stored in SecurityContextHolder
Gotcha: SecurityContextHolder is thread-local, so values do not propagate to new threads or async tasks unless a delegating strategy is configured

chapters.title: SecurityFilterChain Configuration
points: Declare a @Bean SecurityFilterChain taking HttpSecurity and call http.build(); WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter is removed in Spring Security 6
Lambda DSL: http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll().requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN").anyRequest().authenticated())
Rules are matched top to bottom and first match wins, so put specific matchers before broader ones and end with anyRequest()
hasRole("ADMIN") checks authority ROLE_ADMIN, while hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN") needs the full string; do not add the ROLE_ prefix inside hasRole
Multiple chains: use securityMatcher("/api/**") plus @Order so an API chain (stateless) and a web chain (form login) coexist

chapters.title: Password Encoding
points: Never store plain or fast-hashed (MD5, SHA-1) passwords; use an adaptive salted hash via PasswordEncoder.encode and matches
BCryptPasswordEncoder is the standard bean (default strength 10, salt embedded in the hash); Argon2 and SCrypt are memory-hard alternatives
DelegatingPasswordEncoder (PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder) stores hashes as {bcrypt}... so algorithms can be upgraded without breaking old hashes
Hashing is one-way: compare with encoder.matches(raw, stored), never re-encode and compare strings, since each encode yields a different salt
Gotcha: a missing PasswordEncoder bean or a stored hash lacking the {id} prefix throws 'There is no PasswordEncoder mapped for the id null'

chapters.title: JWT Stateless Authentication
points: JWT = header.payload.signature (Base64URL, signed not encrypted), with claims such as sub, exp, iat and roles; never put secrets in the payload
Stateless config: sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS)) plus csrf disabled for token-only APIs
Login endpoint authenticates via AuthenticationManager.authenticate(UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken) and returns a signed token with a short exp

Custom OncePerRequestFilter reads the Authorization: Bearer <token> header, validates signature and expiry, builds an Authentication, sets it in SecurityContextHolder, and is registered with addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)
Trade-off: no server session means easy horizontal scaling but no instant revocation, so use short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens; the signing key must be strong and kept in config, not code

chapters.title: Method Security, CORS and CSRF
points: Enable with @EnableMethodSecurity (replaces @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity); then @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") and @PostAuthorize check access before or after the method runs

SpEL can reference arguments and the principal: @PreAuthorize("#id == authentication.principal.id") for owner-only access; it works only on calls through the Spring proxy, so self-invocation is not checked

CORS is a browser rule enforced via response headers; enable with http.cors(withDefaults()) and a CorsConfigurationSource bean; the preflight OPTIONS request must pass without credentials, and allowCredentials(true) cannot be combined with allowedOrigins "*"
CSRF protects cookie/session-based apps by requiring a token on state-changing requests (POST/PUT/DELETE); it is on by default and can be disabled only for stateless header-token APIs
Gotcha: CORS errors are often really 401/403 from security blocking preflight; CORS is not an authentication mechanism, and disabling CSRF on a session-cookie app is a vulnerability

chapters.title: Security Cheat Sheet
points: 401 = not authenticated, 403 = authenticated but forbidden
Bean skeleton: SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) { return http.build(); }
Order rules specific to general, finish with anyRequest().authenticated()
hasRole('X') means ROLE_X; hasAuthority is the exact string
Password: BCryptPasswordEncoder or DelegatingPasswordEncoder, always use matches()
JWT: STATELESS session, Bearer header, OncePerRequestFilter via addFilterBefore, short expiry plus refresh
@EnableMethodSecurity with @PreAuthorize; CORS via CorsConfigurationSource; CSRF off only for stateless APIs
